planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, average garden soil in full to partial sun; 'Solar Cascade' is a compact, non-spreading selection of the rare Short's goldenrod introduced by the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden's endangered plant program.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full to partial sun; 'Solar Cascade' forms a tidy, clump-forming mound of glossy deep-green foliage topped in late summer and fall by gracefully arching sprays of bright golden-yellow flowers, distinguishing it from the wild species' more upright habit. Selected and introduced through the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden's endangered plant program as a garden-worthy ambassador for the globally rare Solidago shortii, it spreads by short rhizomes rather than aggressively running, making it well suited to perennial borders and pollinator gardens. It is highly drought tolerant once established and is heavily visited by late-season bees, butterflies, and migrating hummingbirds. Only nursery-propagated plants should be grown, since the wild parent species survives in just a handful of populations in Kentucky and Indiana.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or divide established clumps in spring, in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; grass-leaved goldenrod was formerly classified as Solidago graminifolia and is still widely sold under that name.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun; grass-leaved goldenrod is distinguished from true Solidago by its narrow, grass-like, three-nerved leaves and its flat, almost umbel-like clusters of tiny, lightly fragrant yellow flowers, in contrast to the plumed or wand-like flower heads of most goldenrods. Found naturally in moist meadows, roadside ditches, and old fields across most of North America, it tolerates both consistently damp soil and brief dry spells once established. It spreads by rhizomes to form loose colonies and blooms from late summer into fall, when its wide, flat flower clusters become a magnet for a huge diversity of native bees, wasps, soldier beetles, and migrating butterflies seeking late-season nectar. It combines well with little bluestem and other native grasses in a sunny meadow planting; divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.
scientific_name_note: Formerly classified as Solidago graminifolia; still commonly sold and referenced under that name by many native plant nurseries.
